scenes.title: File Permissions & Ownership
scenes.narration: On Linux, every file carries rules about who can read it, change it, or run it — and understanding those rules keeps systems both secure and functional.

scenes.title: The Three Permissions
bullets: Read (r) lets you view a file's contents or list a directory.
Write (w) lets you modify a file or add and remove files in a directory.
Execute (x) lets you run a file as a program or enter a directory.
scenes.narration: Every file has three kinds of permission. Read controls whether the contents can be seen, write controls whether they can be changed, and execute decides whether a file can be run as a program. For directories these meanings shift slightly, but the same three letters govern everything.

scenes.title: Reading an ls -l Line
scenes.narration: The permission string splits into three groups of three. The first triplet applies to the file's owner, the second to its group, and the third to everyone else. So -rwxr-xr-- means the owner can do everything, the group can read and execute, and others may only read.

scenes.title: Changing Permissions
scenes.code:
chmod +x deploy.sh        # make a script runnable
chmod 644 config.txt      # owner rw, others r
chmod 755 run.sh          # owner rwx, others rx
chown data:data file.csv  # change owner and group
scenes.narration: The chmod command adjusts permissions, either symbolically with plus-x to add execute, or numerically where each digit encodes read, write, and execute for one group. The common 644 pattern gives the owner read and write while everyone else only reads, and 755 adds execute for scripts. The chown command reassigns which user and group own a file.

scenes.text: Grant the least access needed — 644 for data files, 755 for scripts, and avoid 777, which lets anyone do anything.
scenes.narration: Follow the principle of least privilege by giving only the access that is truly required. The wide-open 777 is a security red flag you should almost never use.
